sections.title: What Is the Bible?
sections.body:
The Bible is not one book but a library: **66 books** written, on the traditional dating, over about fifteen centuries by some forty authors. They include kings, shepherds, prophets, a tax collector, a doctor and fishermen. They wrote in three languages (Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek) and in many forms: history, law, poetry, proverbs, prophecy, letters, and the four accounts of Jesus called Gospels.

Yet Christians read it as **one story with one main character**. It runs from creation to new creation, and at its center stands Jesus Christ.

Protestants believe the Bible is *the Word of God written*. Its authors wrote in their own styles and settings, yet God so guided them that what they wrote is what he intended to say. Paul calls Scripture “God-breathed.” This is called **inspiration**. Because of it, Protestants hold that the Bible is fully trustworthy and is the final authority for what Christians believe and how they live.

The Bible also invites questions. It records doubt, lament and even argument with God, and it asks its readers to think, weigh and understand, not merely to accept.

sections.title: The Old and New Testaments
sections.body:
The Bible has two main parts. *Testament* is an old word for **covenant**: a binding relationship of promise that God makes with his people.

The **Old Testament** (39 books) is the Scripture of ancient Israel. It contains the same books as the Jewish Bible, the *Tanakh*, arranged in a different order. It tells of creation, God's covenant with Abraham, the exodus from Egypt, the law given at Sinai, Israel's kings and prophets, and the exile to Babylon. Its sections are Law, History, Poetry and Wisdom, and the Prophets.

The **New Testament** (27 books) was written in the first century AD by followers of Jesus. It contains four Gospels about his life, death and resurrection; Acts, the story of the early church; letters to churches and individuals; and Revelation.

Christians read the two Testaments as **one story of promise and fulfillment**. Jeremiah foretold a *new covenant*, and Jesus said that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled. Augustine put it memorably: the New is hidden in the Old, and the Old is revealed in the New. Jewish readers, of course, read these same Scriptures differently, and their reading deserves a respectful hearing.

sections.title: The Protestant Canon: Why 66 Books?
How Protestants Read the Bible
sections.body:
Protestants share some basic habits of reading:

- **Plain sense first.** Read each passage for what its author meant, in its own language, history and genre. Poetry is read as poetry, history as history, parable as parable.
- **Scripture interprets Scripture.** Unclear passages are read in the light of clearer ones, and every part in the light of the whole.
- **Christ at the center.** Jesus taught that the Scriptures speak of him. The Old Testament is read as promise and the New as fulfillment.
- **Law and gospel.** Scripture both commands, showing us our need, and promises, giving us grace in Christ. Luther thought that telling the two apart was the highest skill a theologian could have.
- **The Spirit and the community.** The same Holy Spirit who inspired Scripture opens hearts to understand it. Protestants read personally but also together, guided by the historic creeds and confessions, which they treat as faithful summaries standing under Scripture's authority.
- **Read to obey.** The goal is not only information but transformation: to know God, trust him and live differently.

Every believer may read the Bible for themselves. That conviction is why Protestants have translated it into more languages than any other book.

sections.title: The Reformation in Brief
sections.body:
By the early 1500s many in the Western church longed for reform. Earlier voices, such as **John Wycliffe** in England and **Jan Hus** in Bohemia, had called for the Bible in the people's own language and criticized abuses in the church.

In 1517 **Martin Luther**, a German monk and professor, published his *Ninety-Five Theses* (traditionally, by nailing them to a church door in Wittenberg). He protested the sale of indulgences, certificates said to reduce the punishment for sin in purgatory. Studying Romans, he had become convinced that sinners are made right with God by grace through faith in Christ, not by their own works or by payment. Summoned before the emperor at Worms in 1521, he refused to take back his writings unless shown from Scripture and plain reason that he was wrong.

The new printing press spread these ideas rapidly. **Ulrich Zwingli** led reform in Zurich, and in Geneva **John Calvin** wrote the *Institutes of the Christian Religion* and trained pastors for all of Europe. **William Tyndale** translated the New Testament into English and was executed for it in 1536.

The Reformation renewed preaching, worship in ordinary languages and the Bible in ordinary hands. It also brought painful divisions and wars, which many Protestants today acknowledge with sorrow.

sections.title: The Five Solas
sections.body:
The Reformers' convictions are often summed up in five Latin phrases built on the word *sola*, “alone.” The tidy list of five was put together later, but each phrase captures what the Reformers taught:

- **Sola Scriptura (Scripture alone).** The Bible is the final authority over all church teaching and tradition. Tradition is valued, but it is tested by Scripture.
- **Sola Gratia (grace alone).** Salvation is God's free gift, not something we earn or deserve.
- **Sola Fide (faith alone).** We are justified, declared right with God, by trusting in Christ, not by our works. Good works follow as the fruit of faith, never as its foundation.
- **Solus Christus (Christ alone).** Jesus is the only mediator between God and humanity. His death and resurrection are enough; nothing needs to be added.
- **Soli Deo Gloria (glory to God alone).** Since salvation is wholly God's work, all the praise belongs to him, and all of life, even ordinary work, can be lived for his glory.

A classic Protestant saying, echoing Calvin, guards against a common misunderstanding: we are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone.

sections.title: How to Use This Knowledge Graph
sections.body:
This app treats the Bible as a network. Every book, person, place, theme and verse is a point, and the lines between them show how they connect. You can start anywhere.

- **Start Here.** Try a book marked *Start Here*, such as Luke, John or Psalms, or follow a guided **Journey** through a subject in a handful of readings.
- **Books.** Each of the 66 books has a short introduction, its traditional author and date, a key verse and a reading tip.
- **Themes.** Explore big questions (Why is there anything at all? Why do we suffer?), core Christian beliefs, the five solas and the good life. Each theme gathers key verses, historic creeds and questions for reflection.
- **People, places and events.** Follow the lives of more than three thousand people and trace more than a thousand places named in Scripture.
- **Cross-references.** Every verse links to others that echo or explain it, so you can watch Scripture interpret itself.
- **Bridges.** Where an honest parallel exists, a Bridge sets a Christian idea beside Hindu thought, showing both real resonance and real difference.

Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible. Read slowly, follow your curiosity, and when a passage raises a question, keep it: questions are often where understanding begins.

storyActs.title: Creation
storyActs.text: In the beginning God creates the heavens and the earth by his word. Everything he makes is good. Human beings, male and female, are made in his image, to know him, to love one another and to care for the world. The story begins not with conflict but with harmony, purpose and rest.

storyActs.title: Fall
storyActs.text: Tempted to doubt God's goodness, the first humans reach for independence from him. Trust breaks, and with it everything else: shame, blame, pain, broken relationships and death enter the world. Yet God seeks them out, clothes them, and hints that the serpent's head will one day be crushed. Sin is now humanity's deepest problem.

storyActs.title: Promise
storyActs.text: God calls Abraham to leave his homeland and trust him, promising land, descendants and blessing, so that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him. This covenant runs through the whole Bible. Abraham's family becomes Israel, whom God rescues from slavery in Egypt in the Exodus, the Old Testament's great act of salvation.

storyActs.title: Law and Kingdom
storyActs.text: At Mount Sinai God gives Israel his law, beginning with the Ten Commandments, to shape a holy nation that reflects his character. In the promised land Israel later asks for a king. God chooses David and promises that his throne will last forever, a promise that keeps alive the hope of a coming anointed king, the Messiah.

storyActs.title: Exile and Prophets
storyActs.text: Israel repeatedly turns to other gods and neglects justice. Prophets such as Isaiah, Jeremiah and Amos warn of judgment, and it comes: Jerusalem falls and the people are carried into exile in Babylon. Yet the prophets also promise a new covenant, a new heart, a suffering servant who bears sin, and a coming kingdom of peace.

storyActs.title: Jesus
storyActs.text: God himself enters the story. Jesus of Nazareth, the eternal Word made flesh, announces the kingdom of God, heals the sick, welcomes sinners and teaches with authority. He is crucified under Pontius Pilate, bearing the sin of the world, and on the third day rises from the dead. Christians believe every earlier promise finds its “Yes” in him.

storyActs.title: Church
storyActs.text: The risen Jesus sends his followers to all nations and pours out the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. The church is born: a new family of Jews and Gentiles, rich and poor, united by faith in Christ. Through preaching, baptism, the Lord's Supper and love of neighbor, the good news spreads across the world, and the story continues today.

storyActs.title: New Creation
storyActs.text: The story ends with a beginning. Christ will return, evil will be judged, and the dead will be raised. God will make a new heaven and a new earth, where he lives with his people, wipes away every tear and ends death forever. Creation is not abandoned but healed, and God's people will see his face.

glossary.definition: Books such as Tobit, Judith, Sirach and 1-2 Maccabees, written mostly between the Old and New Testaments. Catholic and Orthodox churches include them in the Bible; Protestants value them as history and devotional reading but not as Scripture.

From a Greek word meaning “one who is sent.” It refers chiefly to the twelve disciples Jesus chose and to Paul, who were sent out as witnesses of his resurrection and laid the foundation of the church.

The work by which God reconciles sinners to himself, making them “at one” with him. Protestants emphasize that Christ, by his death, bore the penalty of sin in our place, while also defeating evil and showing God's love.

Washing with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, marking entry into the church and union with Christ. Many Protestants baptize the infants of believers; Baptists and others baptize only those who profess faith.
The list of books recognized as Scripture, from a Greek word for a measuring rod. Protestants hold that the church recognized the canon rather than created it.
A summary of the faith in question-and-answer form, used for teaching. Well-known Protestant examples are the Heidelberg Catechism (1563) and the Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647).
Not first a building but the people of God: all who belong to Christ, in every age and place. The word also names a local gathering of believers who meet for worship, teaching and fellowship.

A detailed statement of what a church believes, such as the Belgic Confession (1561) or the Westminster Confession (1646). Protestants treat confessions as faithful summaries of Scripture, always under its authority.

A binding relationship of promise and commitment that God makes with people, as with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai and David. The new covenant, promised by Jeremiah, is established through the death of Jesus.

From the Latin credo, “I believe.” A short summary of essential Christian belief, such as the Apostles' Creed or the Nicene Creed, which most Protestants confess together with Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
The Roman instrument of execution on which Jesus died. For Christians it became the central symbol of the faith, the place where God's justice and mercy meet.
A student who learns by living alongside a teacher. In the Gospels it refers to Jesus' followers, especially the Twelve; today any Christian may be called a disciple of Jesus.

God's choosing of people for salvation and service. Reformed (Calvinist) Protestants teach that God chooses freely, not because of anything in us; Arminian and Wesleyan Protestants hold that election rests on God's foreknowledge of who will believe.
From the Greek word for “good news.” It describes Protestants who stress the authority of the Bible, personal faith in Christ, the centrality of the cross and sharing the gospel.
The period after Jerusalem's destruction in 586 BC, when many people of Judah were deported to Babylon. It became a lasting image of separation from God and of longing for home.
Trust in God and his promises, not merely agreement that certain ideas are true. Protestants describe faith as the empty hand that receives Christ, and teach that it is itself a gift of God.
Anyone who is not Jewish. A central theme of the New Testament is that Gentiles are welcomed into God's people through faith in Christ, on equal terms with Jews.

Literally “good news”: the message that God saves sinners through the life, death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. The word also names the four books, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, that tell his story.
God's undeserved favor and kindness. Protestants stress that salvation is entirely by grace, a gift to people who could never earn it.
Set apart, wholly other and morally pure. God alone is holy in himself; people, places and things become holy by belonging to him.
The third person of the Trinity, fully God with the Father and the Son. He inspired Scripture, gives new life, unites believers to Christ and makes them more like him.
From the Latin for “in flesh.” The Christian belief that the eternal Son of God became fully human in Jesus, without ceasing to be fully God.

God's act of declaring a sinner righteous, not because of the sinner's own goodness but because Christ's righteousness is credited to them through faith. The Reformers called it the teaching on which the church stands or falls.
God's rule and reign. Jesus announced that it had come near in his own person; Christians believe it is present now in part and will come in fullness when Christ returns.

When printed in small capitals in English Bibles, LORD stands for God's personal name in Hebrew, YHWH, often pronounced Yahweh, revealed to Moses at the burning bush. Out of reverence, Jewish readers say Adonai, “Lord,” instead.

The instruction God gave Israel, especially in the first five books of the Bible; Torah means “teaching,” not merely rules. Christians believe Christ fulfills the law, and that its moral core still shows how to love God and neighbor.

Also called Communion or the Eucharist: the meal of bread and wine Jesus gave his followers to remember his death. Protestants agree it does not repeat his sacrifice, but Lutherans, Reformed Christians and others describe Christ's presence in it differently.

Hebrew for “anointed one”; the Greek equivalent is Christ. The Old Testament promised an anointed king from David's line, and Christians believe Jesus is that Messiah, so “Christ” is a title, not a surname.
A short story drawn from everyday life that teaches a spiritual truth, often with a twist. Jesus taught frequently in parables, such as the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son.
The first five books of the Bible, Genesis to Deuteronomy, traditionally attributed to Moses. Jews call them the Torah.
A Jewish harvest festival fifty days after Passover. At the Pentecost after Jesus' resurrection the Holy Spirit came upon his followers, an event often called the birthday of the church.
Someone who speaks God's word to his people. Biblical prophets sometimes foretold the future, but mainly they called people back to faithfulness, justice and covenant loyalty.

The sixteenth-century movement, beginning with Martin Luther in 1517, that sought to reform the Western church according to Scripture. It gave rise to the Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Anabaptist traditions.
A change of mind and direction: turning away from sin and toward God. The first of Luther's Ninety-Five Theses declared that the whole life of a believer should be one of repentance.
Being raised bodily from death to new, unending life. Christians believe Jesus rose from the dead on the third day and that all who belong to him will be raised at his return.
Being right with God and conforming to his good will. The Bible speaks both of the righteousness God requires and of the righteousness God gives as a gift to those who believe.

The seventh day of rest commanded in the Ten Commandments, recalling God's rest at creation. Most Christians gather for worship on Sunday, the day of Jesus' resurrection, and see true rest fulfilled in him.
A sacred sign and seal of God's promise, given by Christ to be practiced in the church. Protestants recognize two, baptism and the Lord's Supper, while Catholic and Orthodox churches count seven.
Rescue by God from sin, its guilt and its power, and from death, into new life with him. Christians speak of it in three tenses: we have been saved, are being saved, and will be saved.
The lifelong work by which the Holy Spirit makes believers more holy and more like Christ. Justification is God's once-for-all verdict; sanctification is the growth that follows.
The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, made by Jewish scholars in the last centuries before Christ. The early church used it widely, and the New Testament often quotes it.

Any failure to love God and neighbor as we should, in thought, word or deed, and the inner turning from God that produces it. Protestants teach that sin, inherited from Adam as original sin, affects every part of human nature.
Jesus' favorite title for himself. It can simply mean “a human being,” but it also recalls Daniel 7, where “One like the Son of Man” receives an everlasting kingdom from God.
An older word for covenant. The Old Testament records God's covenant with Israel; the New Testament records the new covenant made through Jesus.

The Christian belief that the one God exists eternally as three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each fully God, yet one God, not three. The word is not in the Bible, but Christians believe the teaching is.

forSeekers:
If you come to this app from another faith, or from none, you are very welcome here.

This knowledge graph explains the Bible **as Protestant Christians understand it**. It does not ask you to agree. It asks you to listen carefully, the way you might hope someone would listen to the scriptures of your own tradition. Christians believe these writings are God's word, and you will find that conviction stated plainly. You are free to weigh it for yourself.

A few suggestions:

- **Read the texts themselves.** Summaries help, but nothing replaces the words of Genesis, the Psalms or the Gospels. A short book like Mark or James is a good place to begin.
- **Bring your questions.** The Bible is full of people who argue with God, doubt, grieve and search. Your questions are not an intrusion; they belong to the conversation.
- **Notice both echoes and differences.** If you are Hindu, you may hear familiar notes: devotion, grace, the longing for liberation, the call of duty. The Bridges explore these honestly. But real respect means not blurring differences. Christianity makes particular claims about one historical person, Jesus of Nazareth, and those claims deserve to be understood on their own terms.
- **Take your time.** These books were written over centuries and have been pondered for millennia.

When two curious men first asked Jesus where he was staying, he answered simply: “Come and see.”
